<reason>Side A won the central clash: a static current unit price does not alert habitual shoppers that the deal changed, because nobody memorises last month's rate. B's definitional burden was substantially narrowed by A's direct-replacement, regular-price, 60-to-90-day rule and by the principle that retailers already link successors for shelf placement and reorder sales. B never neutralised that linkage or explained why merely enlarging today's unit price breaks autopilot.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Most decisive was A turning B's warning that firms would simply raise headline prices into a concession: visible price rises are noticed without a badge, proving the flag restores transparency rather than merely adding history.</best_rebuttal>
